product: Micron sells memory and storage, not logic: DRAM (HBM4 on 1-beta already in high-volume shipments for its lead customer's platform, 1-gamma DDR5 RDIMMs and 256GB modules, LP5X SOCAMM2, LPDDR5X for smartphones) plus NAND/storage (G9 PCIe Gen6 SSD and 245TB QLC SSD in production, UFS 4.1 automotive) and NOR, which makes it today effectively an AI-data-centre memory supplier with a mobile/auto tail. What a reasonable investor would not have known a year ago: with FQ3 FY2026 results on 24 June 2026 Micron re-cut its reporting into four units - Cloud Memory ($13.77bn revenue, 83% gross margin), Core Data Center ($11.52bn, 87%), Mobile and Client ($11.52bn, 87%) and Automotive and Embedded ($4.63bn, 79%) - and disclosed multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements that management says will make revenue more durable and predictable. The same quarter produced revenue of $41.46bn versus $23.86bn in FQ2 and $9.30bn a year earlier at an 84.6% GAAP gross margin, with FQ4 guided to $50.0bn +/-$1bn at roughly 86% - a scale and margin level that was not in anyone's model twelve months ago.
demand: Demand is moving with price and mix, not volume: FQ3 FY2026 revenue rose 74% quarter-on-quarter and 346% year-on-year while inventory barely moved ($8.57bn versus $8.27bn in FQ2), so the entire increase came from DRAM/NAND pricing and a richer mix (HBM, data-centre DDR5), and the ~86% FQ4 gross-margin guide again implies price rather than extra units. The underlying demand is AI and hyperscaler-led - Micron, Samsung and SK hynix are reported to have sold out 2027 memory supply (Seeking Alpha, 5 Aug 2026) and Micron is reported to be targeting 2x HBM capacity by end-2026 (DigiTimes, 4 Sep 2026) - and this week's dated tape is dominated by that scarcity narrative (Barron's, 21 Sep 2026: memory-chip supply cannot keep up with demand; Yahoo Finance, 17 Sep 2026: Intel's CEO says memory prices have risen over 500%). The counterweight is also dated this week: Barron's reported on 23 Sep 2026 that memory prices may peak early, and analysts moved in both directions on 23 Sep 2026 (Wells Fargo to $1,400, Citi to $1,300).
pricing_power: Pricing power is extraordinary right now - non-GAAP gross margin went from 74.9% to 84.9% sequentially and is guided to about 86%, which only happens if you can raise price without losing volume, and Citi's 23 Sep 2026 raise to $1,300 was explicitly justified by stronger DRAM pricing and undersupply. The strongest evidence contradicting the bull case is that this is scarcity pricing facing a supply response rather than a structural franchise: Barron's (23 Sep 2026) flagged an early price peak, benchmark prices are already up more than 500% (Intel CEO, 17 Sep 2026) - precisely the level that invites rival capacity and substitution - and China's CXMT is scaling commodity DRAM (Barron's, 18 Sep 2026), while the target range of $361 to $2,200 across 49 firms and downgrades from Wells Fargo and Mizuho in the last 30 days show the Street cannot agree on where the peak is. If management is wrong, the specific failure mode is that the multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements are effectively priced off today's spot and get repriced downward as Samsung, SK hynix and CXMT capacity lands in 2027, converting a record gross-margin spread back into a normal memory cycle against a much larger fixed-cost base.
competition: Micron is the number-three DRAM/HBM supplier behind Samsung and SK hynix, and the fight is now for AI-memory share: DigiTimes (4 Sep 2026) reported that Samsung and SK hynix keep a scale edge on HBM even as Micron doubles capacity, while Barron's (18 Sep 2026) framed China's CXMT push as more of a problem for SK hynix than for Micron, i.e. the commoditised end is where Chinese entry bites first. If Micron is right, the specific losers are SK hynix and Samsung (ceding HBM/DRAM pricing and share at the top of the stack), CXMT and other commodity entrants (squeezed on price), and NAND peers SanDisk, Western Digital and Kioxia, plus any module builder or OEM that cannot pass memory cost through. On customers, demand is concentrated in a handful of AI-platform and hyperscaler buyers (the HBM4 lead-customer platform plus server OEMs) - exactly the concentration the new multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements are designed to lock in, with the offsetting risk that customer churn or multi-sourcing takes Micron's share before it takes the industry's price.
team: Yes, there was a real leadership change inside the last 90 days: Micron's 8-K filed 26 August 2026 (Item 5.02) announced that Manish Bhatia, previously EVP Global Operations, was appointed President and Chief Operating Officer, and Dr. Scott DeBoer was appointed President and Chief Technology and Products Officer, while Sumit Sadana transitioned out of the EVP and Chief Business Officer role into Senior Advisor to the CEO. That elevates the operations and technology chiefs and vacates the senior business/customer-facing seat at exactly the moment HBM4 is ramping and the Strategic Customer Agreements are being negotiated, with Chairman/President/CEO Sanjay Mehrotra unchanged and no announced compensation changes for either promoted executive. The thing to watch next quarter is who now owns customer contracting, since the durability claim behind the SCAs rests on that relationship set.
market_strategy: Management says it is investing at record levels in technology, products and supply to meet customer demand - capex net of $7.1bn in FQ3 FY2026 and $19.6bn for the nine months to 28 May 2026, with $2.99bn of government incentives received - while ramping HBM4 now, developing HBM4E on 1-gamma for volume production in calendar 2027, expanding DDR5 RDIMM/SOCAMM2 and Gen6/QLC data-centre SSDs, and signing multi-year Strategic Customer Agreements to make results more durable and predictable. On suppliers, that roadmap leans on a concentrated capital-equipment set (ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, KLA) plus silicon-wafer and materials suppliers such as Shin-Etsu and SUMCO, so tool lead-times, export controls and allocation - not customer demand - are the quiet constraint on the capacity plan, alongside new fab construction in the US and Japan. If it plays out as described, annualising the FQ4 guide implies roughly a $200bn revenue run-rate versus about $130bn expected for FY2026 at ~86% gross margins, and the second- and third-order beneficiaries are the wafer-fab-equipment, packaging and test chain (ASML, AMAT, LRCX, TEL, KLA, Advantest, BESI, substrate makers), memory-linked index products (a $26bn memory ETF was pitched on 24 Sep 2026 as the diversified way to own this), and adjacent AI-infrastructure names that benefit from cheaper HBM per token; if it does not, the same supplier chain and Micron's own $56bn of PP&E carry the write-down.
bull: FQ3 revenue +74% q/q / +346% y/y on DRAM/HBM pricing and a richer mix (HBM, data-center DDR5), with an ~86% FQ4 gross-margin guide; HBM4 allocation is reported at ~20% of NVIDIA's needs (thematic book). 49 analysts track the name; even Wells Fargo, which trimmed its target, maintained Buy.
bear: The entire recent growth is PRICE/mix, not incremental volume -- inventory barely moved ($8.57B vs $8.27B) -- so the thesis is a cyclical-pricing bet, not a share-gain bet. DigiTimes (09-04) reports Samsung and SK hynix retain a scale edge on HBM even as Micron doubles capacity, and Barron's (09-18) flags China's CXMT as a longer-horizon competitive/political risk. Wells Fargo lowered its target (1525->1400) on 09-23 while still rating Buy -- a note of caution into the 2026-09-30 print.
falsifier: The 2026-09-30 FQ4 print missing the ~86% gross-margin guide, or DRAM/NAND spot pricing rolling over shortly after, would falsify the pricing-cycle bull case.
